samples.text:
Nowadays, a growing number of students decide to go to universities in foreign countries instead of studying in their home country. In my opinion, this is mainly a positive development, although there are some problems too.

The first reason why I think it is positive is that students can get a better education. Many universities in countries like the UK or Australia have modern facilities and experienced teachers, so students can learn things which is not available in their own country. For example, a student from a developing country who study engineering abroad can use advanced laboratories and learn the newest technology. When they return back home, they can use this knowledge to help the development of their country.

Secondly, living in another country helps young people to become more independent. They have to cook for themselves, manage their money and solve problems without the help of their parents. Also, they meet people from many different cultures, and this make them more open-minded. These skills are very useful when they start working, because many companies want employees who can work in international environment.

However, there are also some disadvantages. Studying abroad is very expensive, and some families have to borrow a lot of money for it. Moreover, some students do not come back after they graduate, so their home country lose talented people. This is a serious problem for poorer countries.

In conclusion, although studying abroad has some drawbacks such as the high cost and the loss of skilled people, I believe it is a positive development because it gives students a better education and helps them to grow as a person.
samples.why: Clear position · relevant main ideas with simple examples but limited development · mechanical linking (The first reason, Secondly, Also) · adequate vocabulary · several agreement and article errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
It has become increasingly common for young people to leave their home country in order to complete a degree abroad. While this trend brings certain risks, particularly for the countries that students leave behind, I believe that it is, on balance, a positive development.

The most obvious benefit is academic. Universities in popular destinations often offer research facilities, specialist courses and teaching methods that are simply not available in many students' home countries. A medical student from a country with few training hospitals, for instance, may gain far more practical experience at an overseas institution. Moreover, an internationally recognised degree can significantly improve a graduate's job prospects, both at home and abroad.

Beyond the classroom, studying overseas develops personal qualities that are difficult to acquire elsewhere. Students must adapt to an unfamiliar culture, communicate in a second language every day and cope without their families nearby. As a result, they tend to return more confident, adaptable and tolerant of different viewpoints. In a globalised economy, these are exactly the qualities that employers are looking for.

Admittedly, the trend has a downside. Many graduates choose to stay in the country where they studied, which means that their home countries lose the talent they invested in during school years. In addition, the high cost of tuition and accommodation means that this opportunity is mostly available for wealthier families, which may widen inequality. Nevertheless, these problems can be reduced through scholarships and incentives that encourage graduates to return.

In conclusion, although studying abroad can contribute to a loss of skilled workers and is not accessible to everyone, its benefits for individual students and, ultimately, for their societies are greater. I therefore regard it as a largely positive development.
samples.why: Clear position throughout · main ideas extended and supported, some generalisation · logical paragraphs with a range of linkers · good collocation (job prospects, widen inequality) · mostly error-free with minor slips.

samples.text:
The number of students enrolling at universities outside their home countries has risen steadily in recent decades. Although this movement of young people is not without costs, I would argue that it is a predominantly positive development, both for the students themselves and for the wider world.

For individual students, the advantages are considerable. Studying abroad often provides access to specialised programmes, well-funded laboratories and academics at the forefront of their fields, resources that may be scarce at home. Equally valuable is the experience of living independently in an unfamiliar society. Navigating a new education system, managing a budget and building friendships across cultural and linguistic boundaries cultivate a degree of resilience that few domestic degrees can match.

The benefits also extend beyond the individual. International campuses bring together people who might otherwise never meet, and the professional networks formed there can later underpin cooperation between businesses, research institutions and even governments. When graduates return home, they frequently bring new expertise and fresh perspectives with them, which can stimulate innovation in sectors ranging from healthcare to engineering.

It would be naive, however, to ignore the drawbacks. The so-called brain drain is a genuine concern, as a proportion of graduates settle permanently abroad, depriving their home countries of skills that are badly needed. Furthermore, the considerable expense involved means that overseas study remains largely the preserve of affluent families. Yet these problems stem less from international study itself than from limited opportunities for graduates at home and insufficient financial support, both of which governments can address through targeted scholarships and incentives to return.

In conclusion, while the loss of talent and unequal access are legitimate concerns, the academic, personal and societal gains of studying abroad clearly outweigh them. This is, therefore, a trend to be welcomed rather than feared.
samples.why: Fully developed judgement · well-supported ideas at individual and societal level · drawbacks evaluated rather than listed · skilful cohesion · precise, natural vocabulary · wide range of structures, virtually error-free.
